source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ ἔστωσαν τοὺς αὐτοὺς ἄγοντες. Τί οὖν; Ἐπεὶ οἱ πολλοί, διακρῖναι οὐ δυνάμενοι τί μὲν ὕλη τί δὲ θεὸς πόσον δὲ τὸ διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν, προσίασι τοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης εἰδώλοις, δι᾿ ἐκείνους καὶ ἡμεῖς, οἱ διακρίνοντες καὶ χωρίζοντες τὸ ἀγένητον καὶ τὸ γενητόν, τὸ ὂν καὶ τὸ οὐκ ὄν, τὸ νοητὸν καὶ τὸ αἰσθητόν, καὶ ἑκάστῳ αὐτῶν τὸ προσῆκον ὄνομα ἀποδιδόντες, προσελευσόμεθα καὶ προσκυνήσομεν τὰ ἀγάλματα; Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ταὐτὸν ὕλη καὶ θεός, δύο ὀνόματα καθ᾿ ἑνὸς πράγματος, τοὺς λίθους καὶ τὰ ξύλα, τὸν χρυσὸν καὶ τὸν ἄργυρον οὐ νομίζοντες θεούς, ἀσεβοῦμεν. Εἰ δὲ διεστᾶσι πάμπολυ ἀπ᾿ ἀλλήλων, καὶ τοσοῦτον ὅσον τεχνίτης καὶ ἡ πρὸς τὴν τέχνην αὐτοῦ παρασκευή, τί ἐγκαλούμεθα; Ὡς γὰρ ὁ κεραμεὺς καὶ ὁ πηλός (ὕλη μὲν ὁ πηλός, τεχνίτης δὲ ὁ κεραμεύς), καὶ ὁ θεὸς δημιουργός, ὑπακούουσα δὲ αὐτῷ ἡ ὕλη πρὸς τὴν τέχνην. Ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ὁ πηλὸς καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν σκεύη γενέσθαι χωρὶς τέχνης ἀδύνατος, καὶ ἡ πανδεχὴς ὕλη ἄνευ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ διάκρισιν καὶ σχῆμα καὶ κόσμον οὐκ ἐλάμβανεν. Ὡς δὲ οὐ τὸν κέραμον προτιμότερον τοῦ ἐργασαμένου αὐτὸν ἔχομεν οὐδὲ τὰς φιάλας καὶ χρυσίδας τοῦ χαλκεύσαντος, ἀλλ᾿ εἴ τι περὶ ἐκείνας δεξιὸν κατὰ τὴν τέχνην τὸν τεχνίτην ἐπαινοῦμεν, καὶ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τὴν ἐπὶ τοῖς σκεύεσι δόξαν καρπούμενος, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς διαθέσεως τῶν κεκοσμημένων οὐχ ὕλη τὴν δόξαν καὶ τὴν τιμὴν δικαίαν ἔχει ἀλλ᾿ ὁ δημιουργὸς αὐτῆς θεός. Ὥστε, εἰ τὰ εἴδη τῆς ὕλης ἄγοιμεν θεούς, ἀναισθητεῖν τοῦ ὄντος θεοῦ δόξομεν, τὰ λυτὰ καὶ φθαρτὰ τῷ ἀϊδίῳ ἐξισοῦντες.
pass_a_gloss: But let them be the same as those who lead. What then? Since the many, not being able to distinguish what is matter and what is God and how much is the intermediate between them, approach the idols from the matter, shall we also, who distinguish and separate the unborn and the born, the being and the non-being, the intelligible and the sensible, and give to each of them the proper name, approach and worship the statues? For if matter and God are the same, two names for one thing, not considering stones and woods, gold and silver as gods, we are impious. But if they are very far apart from each other, and as much as the craftsman and the preparation for his craft, what are we accused of? For just as the potter and the clay (the clay is the matter, the potter is the craftsman), and God is the creator, and the matter obeys him for the craft. But just as the clay by itself is unable to become vessels without craft, and the all-receiving matter without the creator God did not receive distinction and shape and order. Just as we do not prefer the clay to the one who worked it, nor the cups and gold ornaments to the one who molded them, but if we praise the craftsman for something about them according to the craft, and he is the one who receives the glory for the things on the vessels, and concerning the matter and the arrangement of the things that have been adorned, not the matter has the glory and the due honor, but the creator God. So, if we were to consider the forms of matter as gods, we will seem to be ignorant of the glory of the true God, equating the perishable and corruptible things with the eternal.
pass_b_english: But let the accusers remain as they are. What then? Since the many cannot distinguish what is matter, what is God, or how much lies between them, they approach idols made of matter. Shall we, who distinguish and separate the uncreated from the created, true being from non-being, the intelligible from the sensible, and assign to each its proper name, also approach and worship statues? If matter and God are identical—two names for one thing—then by refusing to regard stones, wood, gold, and silver as gods we are impious. But if they stand far apart, as far as a craftsman stands from the preparation for his craft, what are we accused of? Just as the potter is the craftsman and the clay is the matter, so God is the Creator and matter obeys Him for the craft. Yet just as clay by itself cannot become vessels without craft, so the all-receiving matter, without the Creator God, did not receive distinction, shape, and order. We do not value the clay above the potter who worked it, nor the cups and golden ornaments above the smith who molded them; rather, if we praise the craftsman for the skill shown in them, he is the one who receives the glory for what appears on the vessels. Likewise, concerning the matter and the arrangement of adorned things, the matter does not possess the due glory and honor, but the Creator God does. Therefore, if we treated the forms of matter as gods, we would appear ignorant of the true God's glory, equating perishable, corruptible things with the eternal.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the distinctions made by Athenagoras between matter and the Creator, the craftsman and the material, and the ontological categories (unborn/born, being/non-being, intelligible/sensible). Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.

The Greek text is accurately translated in both Pass A and Pass B. The title 'Idolatry and the True God' correctly reflects the content. All key terms are translated consistently with the lemmas provided. The structure and meaning of the argument are preserved. No errors in citation, agency, or doctrine are present.
